title: Do People Trust the Court, or Just Their Side of It?
hook: Only 46% of Americans approve of the Supreme Court overall — but break it down by party, and the real story is a 56-point gap in how Republicans and Democrats see the same institution.
key_points: The Marquette Law School Poll, directed by Charles Franklin, found 46% of U.S. adults approved of the Supreme Court in May 2026, versus 54% who disapproved.
That headline number hides a sharp partisan split: 76% of Republicans approved versus just 20% of Democrats — a 56-point gap, with independents in between at 39%.
The public agreed with the Court's outcome on 4 of 6 major recent decisions, including birthright citizenship (68% agreement) and tariffs (66% agreement).

Agreement collapsed on two rulings favoring executive power: only 27% agreed with letting the president remove independent agency heads, and only 26% agreed on a campaign-finance/party-coordination ruling.
Franklin's core finding: partisan lenses strongly color how people perceive the same rulings, with Republican-Democrat gaps exceeding 30 points on most decisions touching the current administration.
A follow-up Washington Post-Ipsos poll days later found the same pattern: 46% said the Court decides Trump-related cases on politics rather than law, and just 41% approved of its performance.
content_html: "Do you approve of the Supreme Court?" sounds like a simple question, but the honest answer for most Americans today depends heavily on which party they belong to — and which of the Court's recent rulings you ask about.
extra_html: The Marquette Law School Poll, directed by Charles Franklin, found 46% of U.S. adults approved of the Supreme Court in May 2026, against 54% who disapproved. That topline number hides a much sharper divide: 76% of Republicans approved, compared with just 20% of Democrats — a 56-point gap, with independents landing in between at 39%. Looking at specific rulings tells a similar story with more texture: the public broadly agreed with the Court's outcome on 4 of 6 major recent decisions, including birthright citizenship (68% agreement) and tariffs (66%), but agreement collapsed to roughly a quarter of respondents on two rulings that expanded executive power — presidential removal of independent agency heads (27%) and a campaign-finance and party-coordination case (26%). Franklin's takeaway is that partisan lenses strongly color how people see the same rulings, with Republican-Democrat gaps exceeding 30 points on most cases touching the current administration — a reminder that "trust in the Court" isn't one number so much as a reflection of who currently feels the Court is on their side. A Washington Post-Ipsos poll taken later that month found the same pattern from a different angle: 46% of Americans said the Court decides Trump-related cases based on politics rather than law, and only 41% approved of its performance overall — among the lowest approval readings pollsters have recorded for the Court in recent years, though still short of the 58% disapproval Gallup measured in 2022.
